Seasonal description: Marron feature among the freshwater foods associated with Birak. Their presence connects the warm, drying season with the rivers and pools that support aquatic life.
Mullet form part of the fishing resources associated with Birak along the coast, rivers and estuaries.

Bream are among the fish associated with Birak fishing, and Paarndi is used for black bream in the Albany and Denmark area. These fish are closely associated with estuaries, where fresh and salty water meet.
During Boonaroo, zamia seeds ripen and their fleshy coverings change from green towards bright red. The plant is a cycad that produces cones rather than flowers or ordinary fruit.

Marri's pale flower clusters can be prominent during Bunuru, although flowering can extend from December or January through May. The blossom also provides an important food resource for native insects, making a flowering marri a rewarding place to watch insect activity.
As zamia seeds ripen in Bunuru, emus feed on their fleshy outer coverings. This connects the seasonal change in seed colour with a change in food available to animals.
Australian herring are recorded as plentiful during Bunuru, when fishing near the coast and waterways forms an important seasonal association.
Around Bunbury and Koombana Bay, bottlenose dolphin calves tend to be born between February and May, spanning Bunuru and Djeran. Young calves may be seen travelling beside their mothers.
Red-flowering gum can continue to display red-orange blossom during Djeran, linking the cooler season with a vivid flowering.

Reddish reproductive structures and woody cones on sheoaks are described among the signs of Djeran. Their colour adds to the season's noticeable changes in plants. The flowering can extend well beyond Djeran into the following seasons.

Djeran is strongly associated with the salmon run, when large coastal schools take part in a spawning migration. Fish gather around the south-west, with spawning occurring mainly between Cape Leeuwin and Busselton in late autumn and early winter. Ocean currents then help carry eggs and larvae east towards nursery areas.
White flowers may begin appearing on peppermint trees near the end of Makuru. Flowering can continue from July through December, making this an early stage of a much longer display.

During Makuru, black swans gather around waterways and prepare to nest. Breeding in southern Australia can continue through Djilba, so nesting and young birds may be seen across both seasons. Water availability also matters: swans may remain at permanent wetlands or move elsewhere when seasonal wetlands become dry.

Southern right whales visit southern coastal waters during the colder months, linking Makuru with a seasonal return to the coast. Sheltered bays provide places for breeding, birth and nursing. This continues through Djilba and may extend further into spring, especially where mothers and calves remain in nursery areas.

As inland waterways and catchments filled with seasonal rains, kangaroo features among the land-based food resources associated with Makuru. Kangaroo skins were harvested to manufacture warm animal-skin cloaks called bookas to protect against the dropping winter temperatures.

Jarrah produces pale flowers during the spring and early-summer period. Flowering is better shown across Djilba, Kambarang and Birak, so observing nearby trees gives a more useful picture than a fixed date.

Bull banksia may begin flowering in late Djilba, with its large pale flower spikes continuing through spring and into early summer. The display can span several Noongar seasons. Large, deeply toothed leaves help identify the tree before the flowers appear and make it easy to follow the same plant through the year.

Orange wattle produces bright yellow flower heads during late winter and spring, contributing to the yellow displays associated with Djilba. Its flowering period can overlap Kambarang as warmer conditions develop.
Rigid wattle adds yellow flowers to the Djilba landscape, with flowering recorded during August and September. Its display overlaps the transition between cold, wet days and warmer spells.
As Djilba progresses, developing grass-tree flower stalks can mark the approach of Kambarang. Watching a stalk emerge offers a way to notice a seasonal transition before the full flowering display.

Djilba is associated with willie wagtails raising young in Nyoongar seasonal account. Adults can be busy tending nests and protecting their territory, sometimes challenging much larger birds. Their spring activity offers an accessible way to notice the season in gardens, parks and bushland without approaching or disturbing a nest.

White-cheeked honeyeaters are associated with breeding during Djilba in a Nyoongar account. They feed on flower nectar, connecting bird activity with the surrounding plants. Tjoodik can include the New Holland honeyeater within the cultural grouping, so the language name and a photographed bird's scientific identification need not describe exactly the same grouping.
During Djilba, magpies may be building nests, feeding young and defending their family territory. Some adults swoop when they perceive a threat, but many do not.

The southern right whale association continues through Djilba, when mothers and calves may occupy sheltered south-coast bays. These coastal nursery areas offer a different setting from the whales' wider ocean journeys. Some remain into October, so the observation can overlap Kambarang rather than ending at a calendar boundary.
Possums are documented among the traditional food resources associated with Djilba.
Kangaroo paws contribute to the colour of Kambarang's wildflower season, alongside other flowering plants across the south-west.

Moodjar's bright orange-yellow flowers can appear during Kambarang and continue into Birak, signalling the approach of hotter weather in seasonal accounts. Flowering commonly spans October to January. Beneath the display, this root-parasitic tree connects with other plants underground, adding another ecological relationship to its striking seasonal presence.

Marron are among the freshwater food resources associated with Kambarang. Smooth marron can occur in several colours, including a striking cobalt-blue form, but blue marron are not a separate species. This entry shares its scientific identity with the Birak marron entry while describing a different seasonal resource association.
Dugites become more active as spring conditions warm, fitting the broader increase in reptile activity during Kambarang. They occur in a range of bushland habitats, including drier areas.
Warmer conditions favour reptile activity and foraging, making Gould's sand monitor a suitable animal to watch for during Kambarang.
Tiger snakes can become more active during spring and are often associated with wetlands and other moist habitats. They may also bask during suitable weather at other times of year.

Warmer conditions favour bobtails basking and foraging after reduced winter activity. Their thick, short tails store reserves that help them through colder periods. Bobtails also give birth to live young, adding interest to a familiar local reptile.
